case_analysis.focal_point: Whether First Step Act § 403’s reduced 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) mandatory consecutive sentencing scheme applies when a defendant was originally sentenced before the Act, that sentence is later vacated, and the defendant is resentenced after the Act’s enactment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Section 403 of the First Step Act of 2018, Pub. L. No. 115-391, 132 Stat. 5221–5222 (amending 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) and specifying applicability to pre-enactment offenses “if a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of such date of enactment”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that once a pre-First Step Act sentence is vacated, it is treated as legally null, so at the post-Act resentencing the court is imposing a new sentence after the Act’s effective date; therefore, for purposes of § 403’s applicability clause, a sentence “has not been imposed” as of the enactment date, and the defendant should receive the Act’s anti-stacking reductions for § 924(c) counts at resentencing.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States’ position in opposition is that § 403 does not apply because a sentence “has been imposed” as of the Act’s enactment if the district court entered a sentence before enactment, even if that sentence is later vacated; on that view, the statute’s applicability line turns on the historical fact of pre-Act imposition, not whether the sentence remains valid, so post-Act resentencing after vacatur does not trigger § 403. (Notably, in a separate filing the United States also supports petitioners, reflecting a change in litigation position.)
key_precedents: No specific Supreme Court precedents are identified by name in the provided excerpts; the dispute instead centers on statutory interpretation of First Step Act § 403’s applicability clause and the legal effect of vacatur on a previously imposed sentence.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the strongest textual point that “has been imposed” can denote a historical event fixed as of Dec. 21, 2018, and Congress did not add “final” or “in effect.” But that reading, as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, makes § 403(b) turn on a judgment the law itself has vacated—giving operative statutory consequence to a null sentence in the very proceeding where the court must impose the only lawful sentence. Pepper’s “wipe the slate clean” principle does not supply retroactivity (Justice Kavanaugh is right on that), yet it captures the remedial posture Congress legislates against after full vacatur: there is no operative sentence at enactment, so the resentencing is the relevant “impos[ition].” To preserve institutional legitimacy and avoid overreading, I would keep the rule narrow to full vacaturs (not limited corrections), which answers the retroactivity and administrability concerns without importing an atextual finality requirement.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s “nullity” argument has force as a matter of remedial doctrine—after vacatur, the prior judgment has no continuing legal effect—but it does not answer the textual question Congress posed in § 403(b): whether a sentence “has been imposed” as of a date certain. That phrase is naturally read to ask about a completed historical event, and Congress did not condition the cutoff on whether the sentence remained “in effect,” was “final,” or was “not vacated,” so I will not add those words. Pepper’s “wipe the slate clean” principle, invoked by Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch, informs the scope of what a district court may consider once resentencing occurs, but it cannot be used to rewrite Congress’s separate nonretroactivity line. Johnson v. Mississippi likewise prevents ongoing punishment premised on an invalid conviction, yet it does not justify treating an undisputed pre-Act imposition of sentence as if it never occurred for purposes of this statute’s temporal trigger.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s “nullity” framing is the best point for Petitioner, but it does not overcome the statute’s chosen trigger: § 403(b) asks whether a sentence “has been imposed” as of December 21, 2018—language that naturally treats the district court’s act of imposing sentence as a historical fact, even if later vacated. Pepper’s “wipe the slate clean” principle, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, speaks to the scope of resentencing once authorized; it does not license us to revise Congress’s retroactivity cutoff into an “in effect” or “not vacated” test that Congress did not write. Johnson v. Mississippi prevents ongoing punishment predicated on a vacated conviction, but it does not recharacterize the past occurrence of a sentence’s imposition for a limited retroactivity clause. Given the presumption against retroactivity and Congress’s ability to draft a continuing-validity rule if it wanted one, I would not expand § 403’s reach based on later appellate vacatur.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—that “has been imposed” is a fixed historical fact as of Dec. 21, 2018 and that we should not let later vacatur expand a limited retroactivity clause—has real grammatical force, but it assumes Congress meant a legally void sentence to keep doing work in the very resentencing where the court must impose the only lawful sentence. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively re-anchor the phrase to ordinary legal usage: a “sentence” that has been “imposed” in any operative sense is one with continuing legal force, and vacatur eliminates that force, consistent with Pepper’s “wipe the slate clean” baseline that Congress legislates against. Johnson v. Mississippi reinforces the remedial principle that vacated judgments cannot carry ongoing penal consequences; absent a clear statement, I won’t read § 403(b) to preserve harsher punishment via a nullity, especially where the real-world impact is continued stacked mandatory minima Congress sought to curb. I would keep the rule narrow, as the Chief suggests, to full vacaturs so we respect Congress’s temporal line without turning invalid sentences into statutory gatekeepers.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that “has been imposed” is a past-tense, date-certain inquiry into a historical event—has real grammatical pull, and I take seriously Justice Kavanaugh’s related concern about backdoor retroactivity. But that reading assumes that Congress used “sentence” to include a judgment the law has vacated in full, even in the very proceeding where the court must impose the only legally operative sentence; as Chief Justice Roberts explains, that gives statutory effect to a nullity and makes § 403(b)’s cutoff turn on an extinguished legal act rather than an existing sentencing posture. Pepper may not be a retroactivity case (Kavanaugh is right), yet its “clean slate” description supplies the baseline legal meaning of vacatur that Congress legislates against, and nothing in § 403(b) clearly directs courts to treat a vacated sentence as still counting for this threshold. Keeping the rule narrow to full vacaturs (Roberts/Barrett) answers administrability and avoids importing a finality requirement while still reading “sentence” in ordinary legal terms—as something that exists with legal force at enactment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to press the grammar: “has been imposed” can denote a past event as of Dec. 21, 2018. But that reading smuggles in a further premise—treating a vacated sentence as still a “sentence” capable of triggering statutory consequences in the very proceeding where vacatur requires the court to impose the only legally operative sentence anew, a point Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett rightly emphasize. Justice Kavanaugh’s retroactivity and administrability concerns do not overcome the ordinary legal meaning of vacatur (Pepper’s clean-slate backdrop): absent a clear statement that Congress meant a null judgment to bar § 403 relief, I will not attribute that unusual effect, especially where ambiguity affects mandatory minimum punishment and thus implicates lenity. Narrowing the rule to full vacaturs (as the Chief suggests) respects the statute’s line without letting a legal nullity do operative work.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the hardest point that it is awkward to let a vacated sentence—treated as a nullity for remedial purposes—control § 403(b), and Pepper’s “wipe the slate clean” language captures the resentencing posture. But as Justice Thomas explains, § 403(b) adopts a date-certain, past-tense trigger (“has … been imposed” as of Dec. 21, 2018) that most naturally asks a historical question about what occurred in the district court, not whether that sentence later retained legal force, and Congress conspicuously did not use “final,” “in effect,” or “not vacated.” Pepper and Johnson v. Mississippi (invoked by the Chief and Justice Barrett) inform the scope and consequences of vacatur once resentencing occurs, but they do not clearly authorize converting Congress’s administrable temporal cutoff into a continuing-validity test, and the presumption against retroactivity counsels against expanding § 403’s limited retroactivity on that basis. On my institutionalist, text-and-precedent approach, the better course is to adhere to the statute’s chosen line and leave any broader retroactivity to Congress.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s best point remains that “has been imposed” is past tense and can be read as a purely historical fact, and I take seriously Justice Kavanaugh’s warning that Pepper is not a retroactivity decision. But as Chief Justice Roberts frames it, the statute’s trigger turns on whether a “sentence” “has been imposed,” and in ordinary legal usage a vacated sentence is not merely unenforceable—it is treated as void for purposes of the very proceeding in which the court must impose the only legally operative sentence. Without a clear textual instruction to give continuing statutory effect to a null judgment, I read § 403(b) to incorporate that background remedial meaning of vacatur; otherwise we make the applicability of § 403 hinge on an “imposed” sentence the law says no longer exists. I would, however, adopt the Chief’s narrowing principle: limit the holding to full vacaturs, not ministerial corrections, to respect Congress’s temporal line while avoiding reliance on a legal nullity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the best opposing point that “has been imposed” is a past-tense, date-certain historical fact, and they warn that treating vacatur as changing that fact risks backdoor retroactivity. But in the resentencing posture Congress addressed, the relevant question is not whether a sentence once occurred, but whether there is a legally operative sentence that can do continuing statutory work; as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, full vacatur “wipes the slate clean,” so treating a null sentence as still “imposed” makes § 403(b) turn on a legal non-entity in the very proceeding where the court must impose the only valid sentence. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability concern does not move me because the narrow rule Roberts proposes—§ 403 applies when the pre-Act sentence was vacated in full, not when merely corrected—tracks ordinary remedial doctrine and avoids happenstance-driven perpetuation of stacked mandatory minimums Congress repudiated. On a pragmatic, fairness-centered approach, absent a clear statement that Congress meant vacated sentences to remain disqualifying, I cannot read § 403(b) to preserve harsher punishment based on a void judgment.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 403(b) applies to pre-enactment offenses only “if a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of such date of enactment.” When a pre-Act sentence is vacated, it is treated as legally void, leaving no valid “sentence” in place and requiring the district court to impose a new sentence at the post-Act resentencing; reading “sentence” to mean a legally operative sentence best fits ordinary usage and avoids making applicability turn on a nullified judgment. That interpretation is also the narrower, legitimacy-preserving course because it hews closely to Congress’s chosen line (imposition of sentence) rather than importing a finality rule Congress did not write, and it maintains administrable treatment of vacatur in resentencing. See First Step Act § 403(b), 132 Stat. 5222; Johnson v. Mississippi, 486 U.S. 578, 585 (1988) (a vacated conviction cannot continue to carry legal consequences).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 403(b) makes its amendment applicable to pre-enactment offenses only “if a sentence for the offense has not been imposed” as of December 21, 2018, and the most natural, textual reading treats “imposed” as a historical fact—whether the district court had entered a sentence by that date—rather than a later assessment of that sentence’s continuing validity after appellate vacatur. Congress could have written “if no sentence is in effect” or “if the sentence has not become final,” but it did not, and courts must apply the statute as written. While some courts reason that vacatur renders the prior sentence void ab initio, that judge-made remedial doctrine cannot rewrite the clear applicability line Congress chose for a statute that otherwise is not retroactive. Under a strict textualist approach, the reduced § 924(c) scheme therefore does not apply where any sentence was imposed before enactment, even if later vacated and the defendant is resentenced after enactment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 403(b) draws a clear applicability line: the amended § 924(c) scheme applies to pre-enactment offenses only “if a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” December 21, 2018. On the ordinary meaning of “has been imposed,” the relevant inquiry is the historical fact whether the district court imposed a sentence by that date; later vacatur does not change that a sentence was imposed, and reading vacatur to erase that fact effectively expands § 403’s retroactivity beyond what Congress specified. This interpretation respects the statute’s text and Congress’s evident choice to limit retroactive relief, and it avoids the practical consequence of routinely reopening mandatory-minimum sentences in ways that undermine finality and law-enforcement interests. Although Pepper v. United States recognizes that resentencing after vacatur can proceed on a “clean slate,” it does not answer the distinct retroactivity question here, and § 403(b)’s text should control.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 403(b) of the First Step Act makes the anti-stacking amendment applicable to pre-enactment offenses if “a sentence for the offense has not been imposed” as of the Act’s enactment; when a pre-Act sentence is vacated, it is legally void and cannot count as a sentence that “has been imposed” for that offense. This Court has explained that vacatur “wipe[s] the slate clean,” requiring resentencing on a clean record and restoring the parties to the status quo ante. Pepper v. United States, 562 U.S. 476, 507 (2011). Reading § 403 to deny relief after vacatur would give continuing legal effect to a null judgment and would perpetuate the very draconian stacked § 924(c) sentences Congress sought to remedy, with especially harsh consequences for vulnerable defendants at resentencing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 403(b) applies to pre-enactment offenses only “if a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” December 21, 2018, and a vacated sentence is treated as a legal nullity for purposes of further proceedings. When an appellate court sets aside a sentence and remands for resentencing, resentencing proceeds de novo, “effectively wip[ing] the slate clean,” so the defendant stands before the court for a new imposition of sentence after the Act’s enactment. Reading “has not been imposed” to exclude vacated sentences fits ordinary usage, respects Congress’s finality line (protecting sentences that remain in place), and is more workable and coherent than turning on the historical fact of an invalidated judgment. Accordingly, at a post-Act resentencing following vacatur, § 403’s anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) applies.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 403(b) applies to a pre-enactment offense only if “a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” December 21, 2018; when a pre-Act sentence is vacated, it is treated as a legal nullity, so at a post-Act resentencing the court is imposing the only operative sentence anew. Congress legislates against settled background principles, and absent a clear statement to the contrary we presume vacatur “wipes the slate clean,” making the case functionally pending rather than final. Pepper v. United States confirms that after vacatur a resentencing proceeds de novo, which fits the ordinary textual understanding that no sentence “has been imposed” as of the enactment date once the earlier sentence no longer has legal effect. Nothing in § 403 signals an intent to preserve pre-Act § 924(c) stacking for defendants whose sentences have been set aside, and any lingering ambiguity about increased mandatory punishment should be resolved consistently with lenity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 403’s applicability clause turns on whether “a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” the Act’s enactment date, and the most natural reading treats “imposed” as a historical fact—whether the district court entered a sentence—not whether that sentence later remained valid after appellate vacatur. Pepper’s “slate wiped clean” language concerns the scope of resentencing discretion after vacatur, not a statutory retroactivity rule, and Pepper itself recognizes the pre-vacatur judgment was “a sentence” (562 U.S. at 490, 507). Given Congress’s choice of a clear temporal line in § 403 and the strong presumption against retroactivity absent a clear statement, judicial restraint counsels applying § 403 only where no sentence had been imposed at all by the enactment date. That reading is also more administrable and stabilizing for finality and uniformity than tying § 403’s applicability to later appellate developments.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 403(b) applies to a pre-enactment offense “if a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” December 21, 2018. When a defendant’s pre-Act sentence is vacated, the sentence is stripped of legal effect and the case returns for a new sentencing; at that point, the court is imposing a sentence after the Act’s effective date, so the ordinary textual reading is that no operative sentence “has been imposed” as of enactment. That understanding coheres with the background legal principle that vacatur eliminates the legal validity of the earlier judgment, a principle this Court applied in Johnson v. Mississippi when it refused to allow ongoing punishment to rest on a conviction later vacated. It also fits Congress’s evident finality-based line: defendants with still-valid, final pre-Act sentences are excluded, but defendants whose sentences have been set aside and must be reimposed are situated like other post-Act sentencings and should receive § 403’s anti-stacking rule.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 403(b) makes the anti-stacking amendment applicable to pre-enactment offenses “if a sentence for the offense has not been imposed” as of the enactment date, and under settled background principles a vacated sentence is treated as void—placing the defendant in the posture of having no valid sentence until resentencing. Congress legislates against those common-law presumptions absent a clear contrary indication, and nothing in § 403(b)’s text evidences an intent to treat an invalidated, vacated sentence as still “imposed.” Astoria Fed. Sav. & Loan Ass’n v. Solimino supports applying such background adjudicatory principles unless displaced, and the contrast with statutes like 18 U.S.C. § 3742(g)—where Congress expressly keys resentencing to the prior sentencing date—underscores that Congress did not do so here. That reading also advances practical fairness by ensuring defendants resentenced after enactment receive Congress’s remedial reduction of excessive § 924(c) stacking.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether First Step Act § 403’s reduced § 924(c) mandatory consecutive sentencing scheme applies when a defendant was sentenced before the Act, that sentence was later vacated, and the defendant is resentenced after the Act’s enactment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: First Step Act of 2018, § 403 (amending 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) and providing that the change applies to pre-Act offenses only “if a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” the Act’s enactment date).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that once a pre-Act sentence is judicially vacated, it is treated as a legal nullity; therefore, at the post-Act resentencing the court is imposing a sentence anew, meaning “a sentence … has not been imposed” as of the Act’s enactment for purposes of § 403’s applicability clause. They contend this reading best fits ordinary usage and longstanding resentencing principles (a vacated sentence no longer exists), avoids arbitrary disparities between similarly situated defendants based on timing and procedural happenstance, and better effectuates Congress’s core purpose in § 403—ending harsh “stacking” of § 924(c) enhancements for first-time offenders. Amici (including NACDL, bipartisan Senators, several States, and civil-liberties organizations) emphasize that Congress aimed to correct excessive penalties, and that denying § 403 at resentencing entrenches the very stacking scheme Congress repudiated and produces irrational sentencing outcomes.
case_analysis.respondent_position: In the materials provided, the United States’ merits stance is unusual: it filed a brief “for respondent supporting petitioners,” agreeing that § 403 should apply at a post-Act resentencing after vacatur of a pre-Act sentence. The government’s position in opposition at the cert stage (as reflected by the ‘Brief for the United States in Opposition’) was that certiorari should be denied, but the central interpretive dispute is framed as whether the historical fact that a sentence was once imposed before enactment forecloses § 403, even if that sentence is later vacated. The contrary position (adopted by the Fifth Circuit below) treats the pre-Act imposition as satisfying the statute’s ‘has not been imposed’ language, so § 403 would not apply at resentencing because a sentence had in fact been imposed as of the enactment date, even if later undone.
key_precedents: Deal v. United States (1993) (interpretation of § 924(c) ‘second or subsequent’ convictions and the pre-First Step Act stacking regime)

General federal resentencing/vacatur principle that a vacated sentence is treated as having no legal effect (often described as a ‘nullity’), as invoked in petitioners’ and amici’s arguments (specific case names not provided in the excerpts)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that “has … been imposed as of” can be read as a historical fact satisfied once a district court pronounced sentence before the Act, and Pepper is not an effective-date case. But that reading asks an annulled judgment to do present legal work, and as Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, our settled resentencing doctrine treats full vacatur as wiping the slate clean—leaving no operative “sentence … imposed” for the applicability clause to latch onto. A minimalist resolution is to hold only that where the pre-Act sentence was vacated in full and the district court is conducting a de novo resentencing, § 403 applies because, as of enactment, there is no legally extant sentence to carry forward; that narrows the retroactivity concern Alito raises while respecting Congress’s cutoff. Pepper matters not as a direct construction of § 403(b), but as confirmation of the clean-slate nature of resentencing after vacatur, which makes the text’s present-perfect phrasing more naturally keyed to the existence of a valid sentence rather than a historical utterance later declared void.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s historical-fact reading gives operative legal effect to a sentence the law has already declared void, and that is a poor fit with the text’s present-perfect condition (“has … been imposed”) as used in a statute governing which sentencing regime applies. Congress legislates against the settled backdrop that vacatur restores the status quo ante, so—consistent with Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s point—a defendant whose sentence has been fully vacated stands as not yet sentenced for purposes of what law governs the new imposition of sentence. Pepper does not control the effective-date question, but it confirms the de novo nature of resentencing after vacatur and thus supports reading “imposed” to mean a legally operative sentence, not an annulled historical artifact. Nothing in § 403(b) clearly commands preserving the repudiated stacking regime after the prior judgment has been wiped away.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take seriously Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s reliance on the vacatur-as-nullity “clean slate” backdrop, but that background rule cannot displace Congress’s explicit effective-date trigger: whether a sentence “has … been imposed as of” December 21, 2018 is naturally satisfied once the district court actually imposed a sentence before that date, even if it is later vacated. Pepper, which several colleagues invoke, describes the scope of discretion at resentencing; it does not purport to redefine the historical fact of prior imposition for an applicability clause, nor does it authorize reading “has been imposed” to mean “is currently operative” when Congress did not say that. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability and disparity concerns are real, but Congress drew a bright line keyed to imposition, and adopting a vacatur-only exception risks inviting litigation over the breadth of vacatur and destabilizing settled sentencing judgments. Under a textualist approach attentive to practical consequences, the better reading is that § 403(b) turns on whether a sentence was imposed by that date, not on later appellate developments.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s historical-fact reading of “has … been imposed” is the strongest counter, but it effectively gives ongoing legal force to a sentence the law has declared void, which is hard to square with our settled vacatur-as-nullity framework. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas persuasively ground the analysis in that background rule: once the pre-Act sentence is vacated in full, the defendant stands before the court without an operative sentence, and the court is imposing the only legally effective sentence anew. Pepper may not be an effective-date case, but as Justice Kagan notes it confirms the de novo reality of resentencing after vacatur, making it textually coherent to treat § 403(b) as keyed to whether a valid sentence exists as of the enactment date. Pragmatically, Alito’s approach would preserve Congress’s repudiated stacking regime for a subset of defendants based on appellate timing happenstance—an arbitrary disparity I do not think Congress clearly commanded in § 403(b).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best textual point remains that “has … been imposed as of” can be read as a completed historical fact satisfied once sentence was pronounced pre-Act, and Congress could have written “in effect” or “final” if it meant otherwise. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress legislates against the settled resentencing backdrop that a vacated sentence is a legal nullity and the court is imposing the operative sentence anew; in that context, treating a void judgment as still a “sentence … imposed” for an applicability clause is an awkward, legally artificial use of the term. Pepper does not directly decide an effective-date question, as Justice Alito notes, but it matters to the coherence of the text in context by confirming the de novo character of resentencing after vacatur—making it natural to ask whether any legally extant sentence “has been imposed” as of enactment. Pragmatically, the Chief’s narrow vacatur-only rule provides a workable, administrable line that respects Congress’s cutoff without freezing in place a repudiated stacking regime based on appellate timing happenstance.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is textual: “has … been imposed” might be read as a past historical event, and Congress could have written “in effect” or “final” if it meant to exclude later-vacated sentences. But, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress legislates against the settled legal rule that vacatur renders the prior sentence a nullity and the court must impose sentence anew; in that legal context, asking whether a sentence “has not been imposed as of” the enactment date most naturally refers to whether any legally operative sentence existed then. Pepper doesn’t rewrite § 403(b), but it matters in the way Justice Thomas notes: it confirms resentencing after vacatur proceeds on a clean slate, making it awkward to treat a voided judgment as still doing applicability work. Alito’s administrability/retroactivity concerns are better handled with the narrow vacatur-only rule Roberts proposes, which honors Congress’s cutoff without attributing continuing legal effect to a judgment the law has erased.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is textual: “has … been imposed” can be read as a purely historical fact, and Congress could have written “in effect” or “final.” But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett that Congress legislates against the settled vacatur-as-nullity backdrop, and in our resentencing practice (as Pepper describes), a full vacatur restores a clean slate and requires the district court to impose the operative sentence anew under the governing framework. Alito’s reading would make a legally void judgment continue to do work in an applicability clause, producing timing-driven disparities and administrability problems without a clear textual command to depart from that settled doctrine. I would keep the holding narrow, as the Chief suggests, to cases of full vacatur and de novo resentencing, which respects Congress’s cutoff while applying § 403 to the actual sentencing proceeding now occurring.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s historical-fact reading has real textual force—Congress could have asked whether a sentence was “in effect” or “final,” and it instead used the present perfect, “has … been imposed,” tied to a date. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, Congress legislates against the settled legal consequence of vacatur: a vacated sentence is a nullity, and in our resentencing cases the defendant returns to court without an operative sentence, with the district court required to impose sentence anew. That backdrop makes it difficult, as a matter of ordinary legal meaning, to treat a void judgment as still satisfying an applicability condition that determines what law governs the operative sentencing proceeding. Keeping the rule narrow—limited to full vacatur and de novo resentencing, as the Chief suggests—answers Alito’s retroactivity/instability concern without rewriting § 403(b).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to press that “has … been imposed as of” can be read as a historical event, and that Congress could have written “in effect” or “final” if it wanted a different trigger. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress legislates against the settled resentencing backdrop that a vacated sentence is a legal nullity; treating a voided judgment as still doing operative work in § 403(b) makes the statute turn on appellate timing happenstance in a way that undermines procedural fairness and produces arbitrary disparities. Pepper, as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan note, doesn’t decide the effective-date question, but it corroborates the de novo reality of resentencing after vacatur—what matters is whether an operative sentence exists to carry forward at the relevant time, not whether a now-null sentence once existed historically. Alito’s instability/relitigation concern is mitigated by the narrow vacatur-only rule Roberts describes, which respects Congress’s cutoff while applying the current sentencing framework only when the prior sentence has been wiped away.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 403(b) turns on whether “a sentence for the offense has not been imposed” as of the Act’s enactment, and when a pre-Act sentence is vacated the defendant returns for resentencing without an operative sentence in place, so the court is imposing the sentence anew. Our resentencing cases treat vacatur as wiping the slate clean for purposes of the new sentencing proceeding, allowing the court to apply the law governing the sentence it is imposing at that time. Reading § 403(b) to exclude defendants whose pre-Act sentences were later vacated would create arbitrary disparities based on procedural happenstance and is not compelled by the text, especially given Congress’s targeted reform of § 924(c) stacking. This narrower, administrable rule—apply § 403 at post-Act resentencings where the prior sentence has been vacated—fits the ordinary operation of resentencing while respecting Congress’s express retroactivity line.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 403(b) applies to pre-Act offenses only when “a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” December 21, 2018; under longstanding legal usage, once a sentence is vacated it is treated as having no legal effect, so at resentencing the court is imposing a sentence anew and the defendant falls within the text’s “has not been imposed” condition. Our resentencing cases treat vacatur as wiping the slate clean and requiring a de novo sentencing proceeding, consistent with reading “imposed” to mean a legally operative sentence rather than a historically once-entered but now-null judgment. Nothing in § 403(b)’s text preserves the old stacking regime after vacatur, and textualist attention to the present-perfect phrasing (“has not been imposed as of”) confirms Congress drew the line at legally extant sentences, not vacated ones. Deal v. United States interpreted the prior § 924(c) scheme, but § 403 amended that scheme and its applicability clause, read according to ordinary meaning and background legal principles, reaches post-Act resentencings after vacatur.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 403(b) turns on whether “a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” the Act’s enactment date, and the most natural reading treats imposition as a historical fact: if a district court had imposed a sentence before December 21, 2018, the condition for retroactive application is not met even if the sentence is later vacated. Congress easily could have keyed applicability to whether a sentence was “in effect” or “final” as of enactment, but it instead used “has … been imposed,” which is satisfied once the sentence is imposed. Treating later vacatur as erasing the earlier imposition effectively expands § 403 beyond its stated carveout and invites substantial resentencing litigation with serious practical consequences for the administration of criminal justice. Pepper v. United States, 562 U.S. 476 (2011), concerns what information a court may consider at resentencing after vacatur and does not justify rewriting § 403(b)’s effective-date limitation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 403(b) makes the amended § 924(c) regime applicable if “a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” the Act’s enactment; when a pre-Act sentence is vacated, longstanding resentencing doctrine treats that sentence as void—“wipe[s] the slate clean”—so at the time of post-Act resentencing the court is imposing the only operative sentence. Pepper v. United States confirms that resentencing after a sentence is set aside proceeds de novo within the current sentencing framework, and older authority likewise treats vacatur as leaving the parties as if no judgment had occurred. Reading § 403(b) to deny relief based on the historical fact of a now-null sentence would entrench the repudiated “stacking” scheme and create arbitrary disparities among similarly situated defendants based on procedural happenstance, contrary to Congress’s remedial purpose in § 403.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 403(b) makes the amendment applicable to pre-Act conduct only “if a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” December 21, 2018, and when the original sentence is later vacated, resentencing proceeds de novo—so the operative legal reality is that no sentence exists to be carried forward. Our cases describe vacatur as “wip[ing] the slate clean,” requiring the district court to sentence anew, which fits the ordinary reading of whether a sentence “has … been imposed” for purposes of applying current law at resentencing. Reading the applicability clause to turn on the mere historical fact of a now-null sentence would produce arbitrary disparities among defendants resentenced after vacatur and would frustrate Congress’s evident aim in § 403 to end the harsh § 924(c) stacking regime. This interpretation is textually workable, coherent with settled resentencing principles, and best effectuates § 403’s reform without creating an administratively unmanageable timing trap.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 403(b) turns on whether “a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” the Act’s enactment, and in ordinary legal usage an imposed sentence that has been vacated is no longer a sentence in force—it is a nullity requiring the court to sentence again. Our resentencing cases treat vacatur as wiping the slate clean: after a sentence is set aside, the district court conducts a de novo resentencing and must apply the law governing the new sentencing proceeding. That reading fits Congress’s parallel usage in 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c), which speaks of a term of imprisonment “once it has been imposed,” yet (as Pepper explains) does not treat vacated sentences as limiting the resentencing court. The Fifth Circuit’s focus on the historical fact of an earlier, now-vacated sentence departs from the text’s natural reference to a valid sentence and would create arbitrary disparities untethered to § 403(b)’s language.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 403’s applicability clause extends the amendment to pre-Act conduct only when “a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” the First Step Act’s enactment date. Under this Court’s resentencing framework, when a sentence is vacated it is treated as having no legal effect and resentencing proceeds on a “clean slate,” so at the post-Act resentencing the court is imposing the operative sentence anew. Pepper v. United States confirms that after a sentence is set aside, the district court applies the governing sentencing framework at the resentencing, which supports reading § 403 to apply when the only prior sentence has been vacated. That interpretation also avoids an unworkable, timing-driven disparity that would force courts at resentencing to apply a stacking regime Congress repudiated despite the absence of any final sentence to respect.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 403(b) applies the amended § 924(c) scheme to pre-Act offenses only if “a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” the Act’s enactment, and Congress is presumed to legislate against the settled backdrop that vacatur renders a judgment or sentence void—restoring the status quo ante. Under that background rule, when a pre-Act sentence is vacated, there is no legally operative “sentence ... imposed” to which § 403(b) can attach, so the post-Act proceeding imposes sentence anew and falls within the statute’s applicability clause. This reading is consistent with this Court’s recognition that vacatur “wipe[s] the slate clean” for resentencing, permitting de novo consideration at the new sentencing. Precedent concerns cut the same way: nothing in § 403(b)’s text clearly abrogates the ordinary effect of vacatur, and applying § 403 at resentencing best implements the text Congress chose without treating a nullified sentence as legally continuing.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 403(b) makes the anti-stacking amendment applicable to pre-Act offenses when “a sentence for the offense has not been imposed” as of December 21, 2018; when a pre-Act sentence is vacated, it is treated as a legal nullity, so at resentencing the court is imposing the sentence anew and the defendant stands before the court without an operative “sentence” for that offense. Reading “imposed” to include a sentence later vacated elevates a historical accident over the statute’s operative legal reality and creates arbitrary disparities among similarly situated defendants based on timing and appellate outcomes, undermining procedural fairness. This construction also better effectuates Congress’s practical aim in § 403—ending the harsh § 924(c) stacking regime recognized in Deal v. United States—by ensuring that resentencings after vacatur do not perpetuate the very mandatory minima Congress repudiated. The vacatur-as-nullity background principle provides the best fit with ordinary meaning, resentencing practice, and the Act’s remedial purpose.
